Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Vignette:
Minh, a 52-year-old HVAC technician, can pinpoint the exact moment his world shifted. It was a stifling afternoon almost two years ago, deep in the bowels of an old commercial building. He was alone, troubleshooting a complex ventilation system in a cramped, unlit boiler room when a corroded pipe burst, spewing a fine, acrid mist into the air. The chemical, an industrial cleaning agent, immediately stung his eyes and choked his lungs. He stumbled, gasping for breath, the metallic taste of fear filling his mouth as he struggled to find his way out of the suffocating space. He made it, barely, collapsing outside, convinced he was dying. The immediate physical effects faded, but the insidious memory of being trapped, poisoned by an unseen enemy, never left him.

Since that day, Minh’s body had been in a constant state of siege. He was acutely aware of a pervasive tension in his shoulders, a slight tremor in his hands, and a heart that always seemed to beat a little too fast. This wasn't just stress; it was as if every fiber of his being was perpetually braced for impact, ready to react to danger at any given moment. What frightened him most was the realization that he no longer felt safe, not truly. Even when his wife, Lena, tried to reassure him that their home was secure, that the air was clean, he found it impossible to believe her. Her words, though loving, felt naive against the backdrop of his own visceral experience.

This profound distrust of safety manifested in increasingly rigid routines. Before bed, Minh would embark on a meticulous tour of their house, checking and re-checking that every door and window was locked, often several times over. He knew it was irrational, but the thought of leaving even one latch unsecured filled him with an overwhelming dread, a terrifying echo of his own vulnerability in that boiler room. The idea of relaxing felt like an act of dangerous negligence. He had come to believe that if he let his guard down, if he allowed himself to truly unwind, he would be caught unaware, just as he had been before. Sleep was fitful, often interrupted by vivid replays of the incident, leaving him exhausted and even more on edge.

His work, once a source of pride, became a minefield. The thought of being alone in a room or building, especially an unfamiliar one, now triggered a wave of panic. He’d find himself making excuses to his supervisor, declining jobs in basements, attics, or any confined space where he might be left by himself. He started asking colleagues to accompany him on even routine service calls, an unusual request for a man who had always prided himself on his independence. This reluctance to take on certain tasks had begun to affect his standing at work, with murmurs about his reliability reaching his ears.

Beyond his professional life, Minh had also started to avoid anything that could be considered stressful. He stopped watching the news, sidestepped difficult conversations with Lena, and even avoided tasks around the house that might lead to frustration, fearing that any emotional upset would compromise his ability to remain vigilant against a more potent, unseen threat. The accumulated weight of his constant vigilance, the strain on his marriage from his incessant checking and his inability to truly connect and relax, had become unbearable. He felt trapped, his life shrinking around him, and it was this profound sense of being utterly consumed by his fear that finally brought him to seek help, hoping against hope that he might somehow reclaim the safety he had lost.
